title: Blue carbon

definition.text: Carbon taken up and stored by living marine systems, especially coastal ones, in ways that people can manage.

facts.text: Most often the term means the carbon captured by tidal marshes, mangroves and seagrass meadows.
These vegetated coastal ecosystems bury carbon fast because they pile it up in their soils and sediments.
Coastal sediments lack oxygen, so organic carbon in them can be preserved for decades to millennia, far longer than most land carbon stocks.
When blue carbon ecosystems are damaged or lost, they release their carbon back to the air and add to greenhouse gas emissions.
Managing them counts as an ocean-based biological form of carbon dioxide removal, and can serve both climate mitigation and ecosystem-based adaptation.
The term was coined in 2009 to stress that coastal vegetated ecosystems contribute far more than their share to global carbon sequestration.
Seagrass, salt marshes and mangroves are sometimes called 'blue forests', in contrast to green forests on land.

contested_note: Sources say the long-term effectiveness of blue carbon as a carbon dioxide removal method is still under debate.

definition.text: Tidal marshes are intertidal ecosystems of non-woody plants that act as important carbon sinks.

facts.text: Marshes lock carbon in their roots and buried plant matter because sediment builds up fast and decomposition happens largely without oxygen.
Much of their production is belowground, and these deposits can be up to 8 m deep.
Salt marshes cover roughly 22,000 to 400,000 km2 worldwide and bury an estimated 210 g C m−2 yr−1.
They also shelter birds and young fish, protect coasts from storm surge and flooding, and cut nutrient loads reaching coastal waters.

definition.text: The large stock of carbon held in mangrove soils and living mangrove trees, which makes mangroves a major blue carbon ecosystem.

facts.text: Mangroves worldwide stored 4.19 ± 0.62 Pg of carbon in 2012, with Indonesia, Brazil, Malaysia and Papua New Guinea holding more than half.
Of that stock, 2.96 ± 0.53 Pg sits in the soil and 1.23 ± 0.06 Pg in living biomass.
Mangroves account for about 10% of global carbon burial, at an estimated 174 g C m−2 yr−1.
A 2023 meta-analysis found that replanting former mangrove areas stores about 60% more carbon per hectare over 40 years than planting on tidal flats that never held mangroves.

definition.text: Seagrass meadows bury a large share of ocean carbon in their sediments despite covering a tiny part of the sea floor.

facts.text: Seagrass covers only 0.1% of the ocean floor but accounts for roughly 10–18% of total oceanic carbon burial.
Global seagrass meadows may store as much as 19.9 Pg of organic carbon.
Burial rates vary with species, sediment and depth, averaging about 138 g C m−2 yr−1.

conflicts.text: Seagrass covers about one percent of the sea floor and may deliver 15–18% of ocean carbon storage.
conflicts.note: Sea rewilding gives about 1% of sea-floor area and 15–18%, against 0.1% and 10–18% on Blue carbon.

definition.text: Carbon stored in deep ocean waters and the sea floor of the high seas, beyond national jurisdictions.

facts.text: It covers carbon in continental shelf waters, deep-sea waters and the sea floor beneath them, and makes up 90% of all ocean carbon.
It is seen as less amenable to management because data on how permanent these stores are is lacking.
Below about 3 km, CO2 becomes liquid and sinks to the seafloor because it is denser than the seawater around it.
Techniques being explored include seaweed farming, ocean fertilization, artificial upwelling and basalt storage.

title: Seaweed as blue carbon

definition.text: The open question of whether seaweed (macroalgae) forests should count as blue carbon ecosystems.

facts.text: Seaweed forests are strong candidates because they are highly productive and cover coasts worldwide.
A 2016 report estimated they could sequester 173 TgC per year (range 61–268), but the estimate is very uncertain.
Their carbon can be stored by burial in nearby sediments, export to the deep ocean, or as dissolved organic carbon that resists breakdown.
Tracking where seaweed carbon ends up is very hard, so precise estimates of their sequestration capacity are lacking.

contested_note: Sources call it contentious whether macroalgae count as blue carbon ecosystems, since their long-term carbon storage is unproven.

title: Managed retreat

definition.text: The planned, coordinated movement of people, buildings and infrastructure away from places at risk.

facts.text: It can respond to many hazards, including floods, wildfire and drought.
Sea level rise from climate change is drawing attention from politicians, insurers and residents to retreat from low-lying coasts.
Its form depends on the location, the type of hazard and local policies.
Some low-lying countries facing flooding, such as Kiribati, are planning to relocate their populations.
Managed retreat can be very controversial, yet more communities consider it as the costs of adaptation rise.
One New Zealand coastal hazards expert argues retreat is mainly a social and political issue rather than a technical one.

contested_note: Retreat programs have met lawsuits and resistance from residents worried about home values and insurance costs.

definition.text: Deliberately removing or breaching coastal flood defences so the sea can reclaim land and form natural soft landforms such as salt marsh.

facts.text: In the UK its main aim is coastal stability, replacing hard defences with natural soft landforms.
Its big drawback is that land must be given up to the sea, but the new natural areas buffer land further inland by absorbing water and damping waves.
It is also used to make up for lost intertidal habitat such as salt marsh lost to erosion and coastal squeeze.
At Abbott's Hall Farm in Essex, five breaches in an old sea wall let the sea create nearly 280 hectares of salt marsh.
Few sites are monitored consistently, so results have been very unpredictable.

definition.text: Programs in which government buys at-risk properties and relocates or demolishes them, a form of managed retreat.

facts.text: Relocation has been used inland and on coasts after severe flooding and hurricanes.
Sometimes single homes are bought after disasters; sometimes whole communities move, as at Valmeyer, Illinois, or Isle de Jean Charles, Louisiana.

definition.text: Rehabilitating degraded or destroyed mangrove forests so they return to a state like their condition before disturbance.

facts.text: Mangroves provide water filtration, fish nurseries, medicines, food and timber, and protect coasts from erosion and storm surges.
Mangroves store three to four times more carbon than other tropical forests.
Simply planting single-species stands in places thought suitable usually fails, because the soil and water needs of mangroves are not met.
Better methods let damaged areas regrow naturally by secondary succession, provided tidal and freshwater flows work and seedlings are available.
Mangroves are seen as one of the easiest coastal systems to restore because seedlings can survive where no adult trees remain.
Successful restoration would need an estimated US$0.3–1.6 billion per year until 2050; debt-for-nature swaps have been proposed to help pay.
Long-term success depends on support and participation of local communities.

definition.text: The rapid worldwide decline of mangrove forests, driven by clearing for development, aquaculture and farming and by climate change.

facts.text: Mangroves are being lost faster than inland tropical rainforests.
At least 35% of global mangrove area has been lost, and the decline continues at 1-2% per year.
Mangroves make up only 0.7% of tropical forest area but their clearing contributes 10% of global CO2 emissions from deforestation.
Whether a mangrove forest survives sea level rise depends on whether its sediment builds up as fast as the sea rises.

definition.text: Involving local communities in planning, doing and maintaining mangrove restoration.

facts.text: Projects without community support risk backlash and wasted money and effort.
Valuing restoration is hard because most mangrove services are indirect and not sold in markets.
Locals add knowledge of the environment, and paid work and funding give them reason to keep maintaining the mangroves.

title: REDD+ and mangroves
article: Mangrove restoration#Reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation

definition.text: Using the UN REDD+ mechanism, which pays developing-country stakeholders to avoid deforestation, to protect and restore mangroves.

facts.text: The UN launched the REDD program in 2008 to cut emissions and strengthen forest carbon sinks.
In Thailand, carbon markets pay farmers to keep mangroves by making up for the income they forgo from shrimp farming.
